catalog_quote: Barasa (2012) identifies two register tones for Ateso, high and low. Further analysis on the expanded data used for the present study reveals that, at the phonetic level, four tones occur in Ateso: high, marked with an acute accent (´), low, marked with a grave accent (`), a high tone downstep transcribed with an acute accent followed by an arrow pointing downwards (´ꜜ) and a contour or falling tone, transcribed with a circumflex ( ̂) on the vowel. ... All tones are associated with segmental phonemes. They are contrastively assigned to vowels in all lexical elements, meaning that all vowels carry tone. A vowel carries a single tonal element, H or L, or a sequence of two tonal elements, HL. Tonal configurations can combine freely in words; an alternative sequence of high and low tones is most common, with rare occurrence of falling tones at word ends. ... new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (Barasa 2017) classes Ateso as tonal with register tones and gives no stress rule; Tucker & Bryan 1966 agree that the Teso group is tonal (three levels + falling; case by tone) and ADD a placement statement, stress normally on the stem syllable, made for the Paranilotic group as a whole (Teso included as a principal language of the chapter) rather than exemplified for Teso. Tone inventory differs in detail (T&B three levels + falling for the group vs Barasa two register tones + downstep + falling for Ateso) but that is not a stress conflict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement for the Paranilotic chapter (Bari, Lotuho, Teso with notes on Karimojong/Turkana/Toposa, Maasai, Kalenjin): three level tones (High, Mid, Low; Mid often a lowered High) plus a Falling toneme, tone lexical and grammatical (in the Teso group case is marked by tone); word stress normally falls on the stem (root) syllable; only Bari is singled out for grammatically conditioned stress shift and for cases where tone vs stress dominance is unclear; tone/stress patterns vary between dialects. No Teso-specific stress example is visible in the fragments; the stem-syllable rule is stated for the group as a whole.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing on secondary stress in the fragments recovered
new_statements.exceptions: Bari: 'significant shifting of stress in certain circumstances' (tone-class-linked examples not recoverable) and cases where 'it is hard to determine whether tone or stress is the dominant factor'; Observation: patterns 'may vary widely even between dialects' (Nandi vs Kipsigis example).
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's chapter 31 treats 'TESO (with some notes on KARIMOJONG, TURKANA, TOPOSA)' alongside Bari, Lotuho, Maasai and Kalenjin; their Teso data derive from Hilders & Lawrance and Fr. Kiggen-era mission sources (Uganda Teso); the stress sentence is a group-level generalisation, not a Teso-specific description. Barasa 2017 describes Ateso of Uganda/Kenya (Tororo/Busia varieties included).

audit.reasoning: The classification (tonal; no word-stress rule stated) rests on the only modern reference grammar of Ateso (Barasa 2017, Glottolog'sGlottolog's fullest description is a full grammar), which we hold with a good text; the deciding tone quotation and the p. 233 remark were re-confirmed verbatim at the stated pages, and the secondary Hilders & Lawrance 1956 'equal stress.. root syllable perhaps slightly more; stress does not affect pitch or tone' passage was re-confirmed in the held archive.org text. The newer open item downloaded now (Barasa 2018, ATR harmony) is silent on prosody. Remaining unheld works (Tucker & Bryan 1966, Otaala 1981, Schrock 2014 ms.) are older, narrower or unpublished and could at most add an explicit 'no distinctive stress' sentence; none is likely to change tonal-OR-pitch accent.

sources.note: 'Ateso distinguishes between past and non-past tenses: the past tense is marked by a low tone on the syllable peaks of the verb, while the non-past is marked by a high tone on the verb nucleus.. Since tone, tense and aspect are assigned differently in each of the Teso-Turkana subgroups, it is important that they are analysed separately'. Grammatical (tense) tone with H and L; morphosyntax article, not a tone inventory study; largely superseded by Barasa 2017 ch. 3 and tense chapter already listed here. Not downloaded (statement already listed here; not clearly richer).
